newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Hang Seng storms to first close above 14,000.
newsitem.headline: HK's Hang Seng storms to first close above 14,000.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks stormed into uncharted territory on Wednesday as a surprisingly powerful advance swept the Hang Seng Index to its first close above 14,000 points.
The blue-chip index surged 247.12 points, or 1.78 percent, to an intra-day and all-time closing high of 14,153.58.
Analysts said the strength of the rally and the hefty turnover of HK$17.70 billion -- the third heaviest in history -- signalled the market had the momentum to move further ahead.

"The market looks pretty bullish right now and although I expect some correction to take place in the short term, a test of 15,000 looks very likely over the next one or two months," said Alex Wong, technical analyst at Dharmala Securities.
Analysts said a sudden surge in prices during late-morning trade, reversing an earlier drop to 13,830.23 points, had taken them by surprise.
"Momentum is a lot stronger than people thought," said Frederick Tsang, head of research at BNP PrimeEast Securities.
"I think the market can still move up a bit in the next few days. There is a lot of liquidity," he added.

The market received a valuable boost in sentiment when Standard & Poor's said it had raised Hong Kong's foreign currency ratings to A-plus/A-1-plus from single-A/A-1 and its local currency credit ratings to AA-minus/A-1-plus from A-plus/A-1.

The international credit agency said the ratings reflected the strong incentives for China to permit Hong Kong the large degree of autonomy provided in the Basic Law -- the territory's post-handover constitution -- as well as the Hong Kong government's very strong net creditor position and a wealthy and dynamic economy.
Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
"This is a good endorsement that it is business as usual in Hong Kong," said South China Brokerage director Howard Gorges.
Analysts said foreign investors should be particularly encouraged by the move, helping the market retain a buoyant tone in the run-up to the change in sovereignty.
S&P also raised its long-term counterparty credit rating on HSBC Holdings Plc to A-plus from A and its subordinate debt rating to A from A-minus and revised its outlook to stable from positive.
"The upgrade of HSBC reflects strengthening assets quality, which has improved significantly since 1992, reduced leverage and enhanced earnings," S&P said.
The move fuelled a sharp rally in HSBC shares, which jumped HK$6.00 to close at HK$223.00.
"That will have a good influence on Hongkong Bank. It will reduce its cost of funds," said Wong.
He said HSBC and Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd had been leading the market recently and once the lagging property counters began to move, they would carry the index to more record highs.
"It's the banking sector that is leading the charge again. If the property sector joins the party, then I think there is quite a lot more upside," added Gorges.
He said the upcoming U.S. Federal Reserve meeting on May 20 should not cause too many jitters. "When confidence is high here people don't worry too much about interest rates," he said.

Wong said investors were hoping that U.S. economic data due this week would signal that the Fed would leave interest rates unchanged at the meeting. U.S. producer price data for April are due later on Wednesday and consumer price data on Thursday.

Another feature to Wednesday's trading was Beijing North Star Co Ltd's market debut. The Chinese property development concern's shares opened at HK$4.00 compared with an issue price of HK$2.40 and closed at HK$4.675.
